rv.q: For Simon Godwin's production is one of two halves.

“Strong corruption inhabits our frail blood” — so a little humility is always a good thing. On top of that, Shakespeare may not have been mad about puritans because they wanted to shut the theatres and do him out of a job. The great emphasis — indeed, near-obsession — of this production by Simon Godwin is gender, and gender fluidity.

And in general, Godwin’s production is a hoot; while there’s still plenty of impenetrable Elizabethan wordplay, he’s assembled a cast of fine comedy actors that winkle out as much as they can, and fill the stage with daft dancing and fighting, strutting and wooing.
Simon Godwin directs this production, and along with his impeccable cast, manage to wring out every single drop of satire, sarcasm and wit.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this NT production's gender-swapped twist, with Tamsin Greig's Malvolia earning near-universal acclaim for comic brilliance. Godwin's modern direction wrings sharp wit from Shakespeare's classic, though some find the overall staging uneven.
